results.title: Nebius Raises On-Demand GPU Prices Up to 21% From October 1: What an H100 Hour Now Costs | ServerCalc
results.author: ServerCalc Editorial
highlights:
# Nebius Raises On-Demand GPU Prices Up to 21% From October 1: What an H100 Hour Now Costs

Nebius lifted pay-as-you-go GPU rates up to 21% on October 1 — H100 to $4.50 an hour, B300 to $9.50 — the second rise since spring as AI capacity sells out.

October 12, 2026 ServerCalc Editorial 5 min read

The capacity squeeze that has been pushing up VPS prices all year sits at the other end of the market too, on the GPU servers that AI workloads run on. One of the larger listed GPU clouds, Nebius, has just moved its on-demand prices again — the second time it has done so since the spring — and the new rates are a useful marker for anyone pricing an AI server rather than a plain VPS.

## What changed

From October 1, 2026, Nebius raised its on-demand, pay-as-you-go rates across its four current Nvidia platforms. On its own published price list the per-GPU-hour numbers now read: H100 NVLink at $4.50, up from $3.85 (about 17%); H200 NVLink at $5.40, up from $4.50 (20%); B200 NVLink at $8.50, up from $7.15 (about 19%); and B300 NVLink at $9.50, up from $7.85 (21%). CPU-only servers were caught in the same round — the AMD EPYC Genoa vCPU now lists at $0.015 per CPU-hour, roughly a quarter more than before. Separately, from October 8 the provider moved preemptible capacity for these platforms onto dynamic spot pricing, so the cheap interruptible tier no longer has a fixed rate.

These are list prices for on-demand use. Committed and reserved terms are quoted separately and run well below the hourly rate; the increase lands hardest on buyers who pay by the hour with no commitment.

...

The hourly figures are small, but GPU servers run continuously and in multiples, so they add up fast. A single H100 left running around the clock for a 730-hour month now costs about $3,285 on demand, against roughly $2,810 before October 1 — close to $475 a month more for the same card. Nvidia's NVLink parts are usually taken eight to a node, and an 8×H100 box now runs $36 an hour, or about $26,280 a month flat out, up from near $22,480 — a jump of roughly $3,800 a month per node. On the newest silicon the numbers are larger again: a B300 is $9.50 an hour, so an eight-GPU B300 node is $76 an hour, more than $55,000 a month.

The longer trend is the sharper one. In early May the same H100 listed at $2.95 an hour; at $4.50 it is about 53% higher in roughly five months, and the B300 has moved from $6.10 to $9.50 over the same stretch. For a team that budgeted an H100 at spring rates, the single-card line has grown by more than $1,100 a month.

...

Nebius has not tied the increase to the cost of any one component. Its own executives have described a market where demand outruns supply: the company has said it sold capacity as fast as it could bring it online, and that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity on current deal terms. That is the same story driving the memory and storage shortages we have covered from the VPS side — capacity, power and advanced-packaging supply are the bottleneck, and when a provider cannot build fast enough, the on-demand price is the lever it pulls first. A hardware generation that is nominally faster per dollar does not help if you cannot get time on it at the old rate.

...

On-demand is now the most expensive way to run a steady AI load, and the gap to committed pricing is wide enough to change the decision. Treat the hourly rate as the price of flexibility: right for experiments, short fine-tuning runs, and bursty inference where idle time would otherwise be wasted. For anything that runs most of the month — production inference, long training jobs — a reserved or committed term, or spot capacity with checkpointing, is usually far cheaper per useful hour, and the premium for on-demand has only grown with this round.

results.title: Why GPU Cloud Prices Keep Rising in 2026 (and How to Stay Ahead of the Next Hike) | OpenTencor AI
highlights:
If your GPU bills have been creeping up this year, it isn't your imagination. The most visible signal came from Nebius, which put through a blanket price increase across its GPU cloud services effective October 1, 2026, averaging roughly 20% across multiple chip models including the H100 and H200 — its second round of increases since May, according to EQS Newswire reporting on the announcement.

The more telling detail in that same reporting: some Nebius clients have reserved computing capacity as far ahead as 2028, and the company describes demand visibility stretching beyond 24 months. When customers are willing to book compute two years out at rising prices, the sellers hold the pricing power — and they know it.

Nebius is not an outlier. Independent cloud-price trackers reviewed in early October 2026 describe Blackwell cards (B200/B300) as extremely limited with inflated pricing, H200s carrying a premium for memory-bound AI work, and steady upward pricing pressure across nearly every GPU tier. The direction is consistent across providers: up, with the steepest rises on the newest and scarcest hardware.

You did not choose that new rate. A fixed-term contract works like this: the provider sets a new price, and every running instance inherits it on the provider's schedule. results.title: Where to Rent an H100 SXM at the Cheapest Price (October 2026)
results.author: GPUBank Research
highlights:
The short answer, 16 Oct 2026

1. $0.69/hr Cheapest hour you can get. Vast.ai interruptible capacity on a single unverified host in California, at a minimum bid of $0.687 per GPU-hour; the machine pauses when someone outbids you, and disk and bandwidth are billed on top 1. Nebius spot comes next, from $0.79 in eu-north1 2.
2. $1.39/hr Cheapest marketplace listing. A single H100 80GB HBM3 pod on the Lium marketplace in Secaucus, with 8-GPU nodes in Helsinki from $1.69 per GPU; listings appear and disappear as hosts come and go, and no persistent volume is included 3.
3. $1.85/hr Cheapest managed price that includes the whole machine. GPUBank, with 20 vCPU, 125 GB of RAM, a 2 TB local NVMe disk, a public IPv4 and all traffic in the rate, billed per second, or about $1.37 effective after a $100 top-up and $1.16 after a $1,000 one 4.

...

The H100 SXM has the longest price list of any GPU you can rent. GetDeploying tracked 57 providers and 445 price points for the H100 on 15 October 2026, with a median on-demand price of $3.83 per GPU-hour across the 39 providers that publish one 5, and the spread around that median is enormous: the same hour of the same Hopper silicon cost $0.69 as an interruptible bid on Vast.ai 1 and $12.29 per GPU on a Microsoft Azure ND H100 v5 virtual machine in East US 6. Neither figure is wrong. Each one buys a different machine, a different meter and a different promise about what happens when a host fails, which is why the cheapest line on a pricing page so often turns into a bill that is not the cheapest at the end of the month. We read each offer on the provider's own page on 15 and 16 October 2026, and where a page could not be read we name the aggregator and its date.

A good part of the market moved in the three weeks before this page was written, and almost all of it moved up. Nebius raised its on-demand H100 from $3.85 to $4.50 on 1 October and switched its preemptible tier to a dynamic spot price from 8 October 2; AWS now charges $5.97 per accelerator-hour for P5 Capacity Blocks in every region it lists 7; Verda lists $4.17 8, Crusoe $4.50 9 and JarvisLabs $3.49 10, all above the figures of late September, and CUDO Compute, which trackers still show at $1.79, now answers 'Quote on request' on its own pricing page 11. GPUBank, which publishes this page, is one of the providers compared, on the same terms as the others: we say where it is cheapest and where a marketplace listing, a spot tier or a reservation elsewhere beats it.

...

The H100 entered the cloud at hyperscaler prices. Azure's ND H100 v5 has listed at $98.32 an hour for eight GPUs, $12.29 per GPU, since December 2023 6, and Silicon Data's series puts the hyperscaler median at about $7.76 per GPU-hour from August to December 2023, rising to $9.34 in the second half of 2024 41. The fall came first from below. The neocloud wave of 2024 put a median of $2.99 on specialised clouds and $2.58 on marketplaces between June and December 2024, and marketplace rates slid to $2.29 in the first five months of 2025 and $1.95 in the second half of the year 41. SemiAnalysis' index of one-year H100 contracts, compiled from monthly surveys of more than 100 market participants, bottomed at about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 42.

The hyperscalers followed in June 2025, when AWS cut P5 on-demand prices by 44 percent from 1 June 25, which brought the p5.48xlarge to $55.04 an hour, $6.88 per GPU 24; Silicon Data's hyperscaler median dropped to $6.94 that month and to $6.26 in the second half of 2025 41. That was the bottom. By March 2026 the SemiAnalysis contract index had climbed to $2.35, a rise of almost 40 percent in six months 42, Lambda raised its 8x H100 SXM rate from $2.99 to $3.99 on 9 June 2026 43, and in October Nebius moved from $3.85 to $4.50 and AWS Capacity Blocks reached $5.97 2 7.

...

The four

...

### 02 How much does an H100 cost per hour?

An H100 SXM costs between about $0.69 and $12.29 per GPU-hour in October 2026, depending on who sells it and on what terms. GetDeploying's median on-demand price was $3.83 across 39 providers on 15 October 5, and Ornn's daily OCPI-H100 index settled at $3.13 the same day 44. The low end is spot and marketplace capacity: Vast.ai bids from $0.69, Nebius spot from $0.79 and Lium pods from $1.39 1 2 3. Managed clouds run from GPUBank's all-in $1.85 through Runpod at $2.69 and $3.99 and Lambda at $3.99 to $4.29 up to Nebius and Crusoe at $4.50 4 13 14. The hyperscalers sit at the top, selling 8-GPU instances: AWS at $6.88 per GPU, Oracle at $10.00, Google Cloud at $11.06 and Azure at $12.29 24 27 26 6.

...

### 11 Are H100 rental prices going down?

H100 rental prices fell from 2023 to late 2025 and have been rising since. Silicon Data's series puts the hyperscaler median near $7.76 per GPU-hour in late 2023 and $9.34 in late 2024, and the marketplace median at $1.95 in the second half of 2025 41; AWS cut P5 on-demand prices by 44 percent in June 2025 25, and SemiAnalysis' one-year contract index bottomed at about $1.70 in October 2025 42. In 2026 that index rose to $2.35 by March, Lambda raised its 8x H100 SXM rate from $2.99 to $3.99 in June 43, Nebius went from $3.85 to $4.50 on 1 October 2 and AWS Capacity Blocks reached $5.97 7. Cheap hours still exist, on marketplaces, spot tiers and smaller clouds, but they come from choosing the seller rather than from a general fall.

results.title: The Same H100 Costs $2.89 or $11.06 an Hour — Why GPU Rentals Vary Fourfold | ServerCalc
results.author: ServerCalc Editorial
highlights:
In October 2026 the same NVIDIA H100 rents from $2.89 to over $11 an hour depending on the provider — a near-fourfold gap that matters more than which GPU you pick.

October 15, 2026 ServerCalc Editorial 5 min read

Our last piece looked at one GPU cloud, Nebius, nudging its on-demand H100 up to $4.50 an hour. Widen the lens and a single provider's increase is almost a rounding error. In October 2026 the same H100 — the same silicon, the same 80GB — rents for anywhere from under $3 an hour to more than $11, depending only on where you put it. For a team pricing an AI server, where you rent now matters more than which card you rent.

## The same chip, a near-fourfold price range

Checked against providers' own pricing pages in the second week of October 2026, on-demand H100 rates spread remarkably. At the low end sit the specialist GPU clouds: Runpod lists the H100 PCIe at $2.89 an hour, the SXM variant at $3.99 and the NVL at $3.19; Lambda lists a single H100 SXM at $3.99 per GPU-hour. Nebius, after its October 1 rise, sits at $4.50. AWS's prepaid Capacity Blocks for a p5 node work out to $5.97 per GPU-hour. Then the hyperscaler on-demand rates pull away: Google Cloud's a3-highgpu-8g is $88.49 an hour for the eight-GPU node, about $11.06 per card.

A survey of the same pricing pages on October 10 put Microsoft Azure's eight-GPU H100 virtual machine higher still, near $12.29 a card, Oracle's eight-H100 shape at $10.00 per GPU-hour, and marketplace capacity on Vast.ai as low as $1.68. From the cheapest verified list price to the dearest, that is a near-fourfold range on providers' own pages — wider still once the marketplace floor is counted — for a card that is, physically, identical.

...

GPU servers run flat out and in multiples, so the hourly gap compounds into real money. A single H100 left running around the clock for a 730-hour month costs about $2,110 at Runpod's PCIe rate and about $8,074 on Google Cloud on demand — a difference of nearly $6,000 a month for the same unit of compute. NVLink cards are usually taken eight to a node: that is roughly $16,900 a month on the cheap tier against about $64,600 on Google's on-demand node, close to $47,700 a month apart. Nebius's $4.50 lands at about $3,285 a month per card; AWS's prepaid block at about $4,360. The point is not that one number is right and the others wrong — it is that the provider decision moves the bill by more than any chip-generation upgrade or any single provider's price change does.

...

Part of it is what is bundled. The hyperscaler rate buys an on-demand machine inside a full platform — managed networking, identity, support, instant capacity and no commitment — and that convenience is priced in. The specialist clouds sell closer to raw metal: you get the card and little else, often from a smaller region footprint, sometimes on a community or marketplace tier where another customer's idle hardware is being resold.

Commitment is the other axis. On-demand is the most expensive way to run a steady load everywhere; AWS's Capacity Block rate already sits below its own on-demand rate, and committed or reserved terms on any of these clouds run well under the hourly figure. The quoted hour is the price of flexibility, and the hyperscalers charge the most for it. A nominally faster card per dollar does not help if the rate you can actually book it at is triple what a specialist charges for last generation's silicon.

results.title: Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here's how companies access them
results.author: Jordan Novet
highlights:
Key Points

- AI labs are spending tens of billions of dollars per year for Nvidia chips that run their models.
- The demand has led to the blossoming of an industry that hyperscalers once had to themselves, including lucrative one-off arrangements and asset-light strategies.
- Over 300 neoclouds now rent GPUs to businesses, according to a review from researcher SemiAnalysis, up 55% in under 11 months.

...

Customers can now shop around for access to the chips at the giant clouds from Amazon, Microsoft and Google, as well as at so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave. They can also go to various online marketplaces or even buy the costly hardware directly.

...

Industry research firm SemiAnalysis counted 323 Nvidia GPU providers as of September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier.

...

Companies using these smaller neoclouds share the same concerns: When can they get the GPUs, and at what price? Sunny Smith, co-founder and technology chief at Massed Compute, said customers are often willing to commit to capacity when they expect prices to rise.

...

In April, SpaceX agreed to provide Cursor with GPUs and then bought the AI coding startup outright for $60 billion. And in May, SpaceX landed a deal to rent GPUs to Anthropic for $1.25 billion each month through mid-2029. That's more than what most startups can afford.

...

The hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes.

results.title: Why GPU prices spike during AI compute shortages | CloudPe Blog
results.author: Gautami Teliwadekar
highlights:
GPU prices spike when AI demand outpaces the memory, chip packaging, and power new GPUs need. In 2026, NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 list price rose from $8,565 to $16,000, and B200 rentals jumped 79% in three months. Yet H100 rentals fell 64% to 75% from their 2024 peak.

...

A GPU price spike is a sharp rise in what buyers pay to rent or own a GPU, usually within weeks or months. It shows up in two places: hourly cloud rates and hardware list prices. The two can move at different times and by different amounts.

Contract type matters too. Spot and on-demand rates track the market daily, while reserved contracts lock a price for a year or more. In 2026, reserved H100 prices rose about 40% while on-demand prices fell, because on-demand capacity was sold out.

## GPU prices in 2026

Cloud GPU rental prices are up 13% over 12 months across 21 models, with 16 rising and 5 falling. The GPU prices chart below shows the biggest moves. Rental figures are in US dollars per GPU-hour.

| GPU or price type | Earlier | Latest | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, one-year contract | $1.70 (Oct 2025) | $2.35 (Mar 2026) | +38% |
| H100, on-demand median | 12 months ago | $3.57 (week of 12 Oct 2026) | +19% |
| B200 rental | 3 months ago | $8.01 (Sept 2026) | +79% |
| RTX PRO 6000 list price | $8,565 (Mar 2025) | $16,000 (Aug 2026) | +87% |

Note: Trackers measure different things, so the same GPU can show different prices. On 7 October, one list-price median put the H100 at $4.20, while trade-based indexes showed about $2.81 to $2.86.

...

GPU prices spike because demand rises fast while supply cannot. New supply depends on memory, packaging, and power that take quarters or years to expand. With supply fixed, price absorbs the extra demand.

Three forces stack up. Demand jumps when new AI products launch. Supply is capped by a few scarce parts. Contracts then lock capacity away, so less reaches the open market. Prices rise first where capacity is tightest: newest GPUs, high-memory cards and reserved contracts.

...

Cloud providers buy to build capacity: Capex means money spent on data centres, servers and chips. The four largest US cloud providers have guided about $730 billion of capex for 2026, up 78% from 2025. Much of it goes to GPUs, so their orders set the pace for the whole market.

...

GPU prices spike when new demand lands before new supply, and they fall when supply catches up. The record from 2024 to 2026 shows four phases.

| Period | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Early 2024 | H100 rentals peak at $8 to $10 an hour |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | H100 on-demand up 10% in four weeks, from $2.00 to $2.20 |
| Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contracts reach $2.35 |
| Jun 2026 | H100 eases to $2.01 to $2.53 as Blackwell supply ramps |
| 1 Oct 2026 | Nebius raises H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 |

From the above table reading, each fall followed new supply, and each rise followed a new kind of demand or a new bottleneck. The shortage has moved from GPUs to memory and power, which is why spikes keep returning.

...

As of 14 October 2026, CloudPe lists the L4 at ₹35.86 an hour, the RTX PRO 6000 at ₹185.56, and the H200 at ₹410. Billing is in INR from a Mumbai Tier-4 data centre, with no data-transfer surcharges within India. The table converts rates at ₹95 to the dollar.

| GPU | CloudPe per hour | Market median | Hyperscaler | CloudPe vs Hyperscaler |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L4 (24 GB) | ₹35.86 (about $0.38) | $0.78 | $0.707 | 47% lower |
| RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB) | ₹185.56 (about $1.95) | $2.39 | $4.50 | 57% lower |
| H200 (141 GB) | ₹410 (about $4.32) | $4.98 | $10.60 per GPU | 59% lower |

results.title: Every Term You Need to Understand AI Compute Pricing
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
On October 10, 2026, eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs rented as a single node listed at $31.92 an hour on Lambda and $98.32 an hour on Microsoft Azure. Same silicon, same generation, a 3.1x gap. Run either for a month and the difference is $48,472 for one node.

...

+16.9% Nebius on-demand H100 increase, effective Oct 1 Nebius, 2026

...

For most of 2025 the story was simple: prices fell. AWS cut on-demand pricing on its H100-based P5 instances by 44 percent in June 2025 (AWS News Blog, 2025). That era is over. SemiAnalysis tracked one-year H100 contract pricing rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, an increase of about 38 percent, as on-demand capacity sold out (SemiAnalysis, 2026). On October 1, 2026, Nebius raised on-demand H100 pricing from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour and B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, its second increase in a few months (Nebius pricing page, 2026; Stocktwits, 2026).

When prices move in both directions at once, falling on spot marketplaces and rising on contracts, the term attached to the number matters as much as the number itself. Note the source bias too: several widely cited price ranges come from GPU vendors with an interest in making their own rate look cheap. We use first-party price lists wherever possible and say so when we do not.

...

Here is what the glossary looks like applied. Six published on-demand or prepaid rates for one eight-GPU H100 node, run continuously for 730 hours, the same unit CME uses for one futures contract. Rates are first-party list prices checked October 10 to 14, 2026.

| Provider and SKU | $ per GPU-hr | Node $ per hr | 730-hr month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lambda, 8x H100 SXM instance | $3.99 | $31.92 | $23,301.60 |
| Nebius, HGX H100 (from Oct 1) | $4.50 | $36.00 | $26,280.00 |
| AWS p5.48xlarge, Capacity Block | $5.97 | $47.76 | $34,862.61 |
| CoreWeave, HGX H100 node | $6.16 | $49.24 | $35,945.20 |
| AWS p5.48xlarge, on-demand | $6.88 | $55.04 | $40,179.20 |
| Azure ND96isr H100 v5 | $12.29 | $98.32 | $71,773.60 |

8 x H100 per node, 730 hours continuous, 5,840 GPU-hours. First-party list prices, US regions, checked October 10 to 14, 2026. Excludes storage, data transfer and support.

...

- The same H100 node ranged from $31.92 to $98.32 per hour on first-party price lists in October 2026, a 3.1x spread driven by packaging and terms, not silicon.
- GPU prices are moving in both directions: spot marketplaces stay cheap while contract and neocloud on-demand rates rose through 2026, including Nebius's October 1 increase of up to 21 percent.
- Compare effective cost per useful GPU-hour, not list rate. Idle time can erase any provider discount.
- Compute futures on CME turn GPU rental into a hedgeable commodity. Plan AI budgets for commodity-style volatility.
- Keep training data on zero-egress storage so you can follow the cheapest available GPUs without paying to leave.
